The answer is $n^2$ if $n$ is even, and $n^2 - 5$ if $n$ is odd.
It is easy when $n$ is even. Let $k = \frac{n+1}{2}$. Then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}| &\le \sum_{i=1}^{n} (|k - a_i| + |k - a_{i+1}| + |k - a_{i+2}| + |k - a_{i+3}|) \\
&= 4 \sum_{i=1}^{n} |k - a_i| = n^2,
\end{aligned}
$$
and the equality holds when $a_{2i-1} = i$ and $a_{2i} = \frac{n}{2} + 1$ for $i = 1, 2, \dots, \frac{n}{2}$. So, the maximum of $\sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}|$ is $n^2$.

Let $n$ be odd. Without loss of generality, let $a_1 - a_2 > 0$. If $a_i - a_{i+1} > 0$ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, then
$$
0 = (a_1 - a_2) + (a_2 - a_3) + \dots + (a_n - a_1) > 0,
$$
a contradiction. So, there exists $1 < x \le n$ such that $a_x - a_{x+1} < 0$, and thus there exist distinct $1 \le p, q \le n$ such that $a_p - a_{p+1} > 0$, $a_{p+2} - a_{p+3} < 0$ and $a_q - a_{q+1} < 0$, $a_{q+2} - a_{q+3} > 0$.

Now we consider the value of $|a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}|$. If $a_i - a_{i+1}$ and $a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}$ have the same sign then $|a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}| = |a_i - a_{i+1}| + |a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}|$, and if $a_i - a_{i+1}$ and $a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}$ have different signs then
$$
|a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}| = \big| |a_i - a_{i+1}| - |a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}| \big| \le |a_i - a_{i+1}| + |a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}| - 2.
$$
So $\sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}|$ is at most
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum_{1 \le i \le n, i \ne p, q} (|a_i - a_{i+1}| + |a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}|) \\
& \quad + |a_p - a_{p+1}| + |a_{p+2} - a_{p+3}| + |a_q - a_{q+1}| + |a_{q+2} - a_{q+3}| - 4 \\
& = 2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1}| - 4.
\end{aligned}
$$
Let $k = \frac{n+1}{2}$. Then,
$$
2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1}| - 4 \le 2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (|k - a_i| + |k - a_{i+1}|) - 4 = 4 \sum_{i=1}^{n} |k - a_i| - 4 = n^2 - 5.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}| \le n^2 - 5
$$
and the equality is attained when $a_n = \frac{n+1}{2}$ and $a_{2i} = i$, $a_{2i-1} = \frac{n+1}{2} + i$ for $i = 1, 2, \dots, \frac{n-1}{2}$. Thus the maximum of $\sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} - a_{i+3}|$ is $n^2 - 5$. $\square$

statement:
Let $a, b, c > 0$ and $a + b + c = 3$. Prove that
$$
\frac{1}{a\sqrt{2(a^2+bc)}} + \frac{1}{b\sqrt{2(b^2+ca)}} + \frac{1}{c\sqrt{2(c^2+ab)}} \ge \frac{1}{a+bc} + \frac{1}{b+ca} + \frac{1}{c+ab}.
$$
title: Thai Mathematical Olympiad
solutions:
Without loss of generality, we may assume that $a \ge b \ge c$. Then
$$
\frac{(c-a)(c-b)}{3(c+ab)} \ge 0
$$
and
$$
\frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{3(a+bc)} + \frac{(b-a)(b-c)}{3(b+ca)} = \frac{c(a-b)^2}{3} \left( \frac{1+a+b-c}{(a+bc)(b+ca)} \right) \ge 0
$$
Therefore
$$
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{3(a+bc)} \ge 0
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{a+bc} &\le \frac{9}{2(ab+bc+ca)} \\
\Leftrightarrow \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{a(a+b+c)+3bc} &\le \frac{3}{2(ab+bc+ca)} \\
\Leftrightarrow \sum_{\text{cyc}} \left[ \frac{1}{2(ab+bc+ca)} - \frac{1}{a(a+b+c)+3bc} \right] &\ge 0 \\
\Leftrightarrow \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a(a+b+c)+3bc} &= \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{3(a+bc)} \ge 0.
\end{align*}
$$
By the AM-GM inequality, we have
$$
\frac{1}{a\sqrt{2(a^2 + bc)}} = \frac{\sqrt{b+c}}{\sqrt{2a}\sqrt{(ab+ac)(a^2+bc)}} \ge \frac{\sqrt{2(b+c)}}{\sqrt{a(a+b)(a+c)}}
$$
So it suffices to prove that
$$
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \cdot \frac{1}{(a+b)(a+c)} \ge \frac{9}{4(ab+bc+ca)}
$$
Since $\sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \le \sqrt{\frac{c+a}{2b}} \le \sqrt{\frac{a+b}{2c}}$ and
$$
\frac{1}{(a+b)(a+c)} \le \frac{1}{(b+c)(b+a)} \le \frac{1}{(c+a)(c+b)},
$$
by Chebyshev's inequality, we get
$$
\begin{align*}
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \cdot \frac{1}{(a+b)(a+c)} &\ge \frac{1}{3} \left( \sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \right) \left( \sum_{\text{cyc}} \frac{1}{(a+b)(a+c)} \right) \\
&= \frac{2}{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)} \left( \sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \right).
\end{align*}
$$
In view of these estimates, we now see that it suffices to show that
$$
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \ge \frac{9(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}{8(ab+bc+ca)}.
$$
Let $t := \sqrt[6]{\frac{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}{8abc}}$. Clearly $t \ge 1$. Using the AM-GM inequality, we find that
$$
\sum_{\text{cyc}} \sqrt{\frac{b+c}{2a}} \ge 3t.
$$

It is easy to verify that $\frac{9(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}{8(ab+bc+ca)} = \frac{27t^6}{8t^6+1}$; so, it is enough to prove that
$3t \ge \frac{27t^6}{8t^6+1}$ or $8t^6 - 9t^5 + 1 \ge 0$.
Since $t \ge 1$, this inequality is true and the proof is completed. $\square$

statement: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be three distinct points on a unit circle. Let $G$ and $H$ be the centroid and the orthocenter of the triangle $ABC$, respectively. Let $F$ be the midpoint of the segment $GH$. Evaluate $|AF|^2 + |BF|^2 + |CF|^2$.
title: Thai Mathematical Olympiad
solutions:
Define a coordinate system with the origin at the center of the circle. We can see that $\vec{H} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C}$ and $\vec{G} = \frac{1}{3}(\vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C})$.
Thus, $\vec{F} = \frac{\vec{G} + \vec{H}}{2} = \frac{2}{3}(\vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C})$. We now have
$$
\begin{aligned}
|AF|^2 + |BF|^2 + |CF|^2 
&= (\vec{A} - \vec{F}) \cdot (\vec{A} - \vec{F}) + (\vec{B} - \vec{F}) \cdot (\vec{B} - \vec{F}) + (\vec{C} - \vec{F}) \cdot (\vec{C} - \vec{F}) \\
&= |\vec{A}|^2 + |\vec{B}|^2 + |\vec{C}|^2 - 2(\vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C}) \cdot \vec{F} + 3\vec{F} \cdot \vec{F} \\
&= |\vec{A}|^2 + |\vec{B}|^2 + |\vec{C}|^2 - (2(\vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C}) - 3\vec{F}) \cdot \vec{F} \\
&= |\vec{A}|^2 + |\vec{B}|^2 + |\vec{C}|^2 = 3.
\end{aligned}
$$

title: Thai Mathematical Olympiad
solutions:
Define $\lambda(x, y) = \frac{2008}{x^2y^3}$ for all $x, y > 0$.
We can see that $\left(\frac{x}{\lambda(x, y)}\right)^2 (y \cdot \lambda(x, y))^3 = 2008$. Thus,
$$ \left(\frac{x}{z}\right)^2 (yz)^3 > 2008 \text{ for every } z > \lambda(x, y). $$
It follows that $(f(xy))^2 = f(x^2/z^2)f(y^2z^2)$ for all $z > \lambda(x, y)$.
Now for any positive real numbers $x$ and $y$, we choose
$$ z > \max\{\lambda(x, x), \lambda(y, y), \lambda(x, y), \lambda(y, x)\}. $$
It follows that
$$
(f(x^2))^2 = f(x^2/z^2) f(x^2z^2) \quad (\because z > \lambda(x, x))
$$
$$
(f(y^2))^2 = f(y^2/z^2) f(y^2z^2) \quad (\because z > \lambda(y, y))
$$
$$
(f(xy))^2 = f(x^2/z^2) f(y^2z^2) \quad (\because z > \lambda(x, y))
$$
$$
(f(xy))^2 = f(y^2/z^2) f(x^2z^2) \quad (\because z > \lambda(y, x))
$$
We can see that
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(xy)^2 \cdot f(xy)^2 &= (f(x^2/z^2) f(y^2z^2))(f(y^2/z^2) f(x^2z^2)) \\
&= (f(x^2/z^2) f(x^2z^2))(f(y^2/z^2) f(y^2z^2)) \\
&= (f(x^2))^2 (f(y^2))^2
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus $(f(xy))^2 = f(x^2)f(y^2)$ for all $x, y > 0$.

solutions:
Assume without loss of generality that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. By the AM-GM inequality,
$$
c^2 = a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab.
$$
That is,
$$
c^3 \ge 2abc. \quad (1)
$$
Next, we will show that $a^3 + b^3 \ge \sqrt{2}abc$. Consider $a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2 + b^2) - ab(a+b)$ and
$$
\begin{align*}
(a+b)(a^2 + b^2) &= (a+b)c^2 = (a+b)\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}c \\
&\ge 2\sqrt{ab}\sqrt{2ab}c \\
&= 2\sqrt{2abc}.
\end{align*} \quad (2)
$$
Now, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
$$
\begin{align}
ab(a+b) &\le ab\sqrt{2}\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \tag{3} \\
&= \sqrt{2abc},
\end{align}
$$
and so
$$
a^3 + b^3 \ge 2\sqrt{2abc} - \sqrt{2abc} = \sqrt{2abc} \quad (4)
$$
We conclude from (1) and (4) that
$$
\frac{a^3 + b^3 + c^3}{abc} \ge 2 + \sqrt{2}. \quad (5)
$$
This will be an equality when $a = b$.

statement:
Prove that there are no integer pairs $(x, y)$ satisfying
$$
2560x^2 + 5x + 6 = y^5.
$$
title: The 14th Thailand Mathematical Olympiad
solutions:
Suppose for the sake of contradiction that an integer pair $(x, y)$ satisfies $2560x^2 + 5x + 6 = y^5$. Thus, $6 \equiv y^5 \equiv y \pmod{5}$, and so $y \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$. Let $k$ be an integer such that $y = 5k + 1$. We now have
$$
2560x^2 + 5x + 6 = (5k + 1)^5 = 1 + \sum_{j=1}^{5} \binom{5}{j} (5k)^j.
$$
Dividing the above equation by $5$ yields
$$
512x^2 + x + 1 = 5^4k^5 + 5^4k^4 + 10 \cdot 5^2k^3 + 10 \cdot 5k^2 + 5k.
$$
Taking the above equation modulo $5$, we obtain $2x^2 + x + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$. This makes $1 \equiv 2x^2 - 4x + 2 \equiv 2(x - 1)^2 \pmod{5}$, and so $3 \equiv (x - 1)^2 \pmod{5}$. This is a contradiction since $3$ is not a square modulo $5$.

statement:
If $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ are positive real numbers such that
$$
t = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n = a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \dots + a_n^2
$$
and $n \ge 2$, then show that
$$
\sum_{i \neq j} \frac{a_i}{a_j} \geq \frac{(n-1)^2 t}{t-1}.
$$
solutions:
By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,
$$
\sum_{i \neq j} \frac{a_i}{a_j} \cdot \sum_{i \neq j} a_i a_j \geq \left( \sum_{i \neq j} a_i \right)^2 = \left( (n-1) \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \right)^2 = (n-1)^2 t^2.
$$
On the other hand,
$$
\sum_{i \neq j} a_i a_j = \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \right)^2 - \left( \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i^2 \right) = t^2 - t.
$$
The required inequality follows.

statement: Find the largest real number $t$ such that, in any school with $2006$ students and $14$ teachers where every student is acquainted with at least one teacher, a student and a teacher can be found such that they are acquainted with each other, and the ratio of the number of students who are acquainted with the teacher to the number of teachers who are acquainted with the student is at least $t$.
title: 14th Turkish Mathematical Olympiad
solutions:
$t = 2006/14$.
If every student is acquainted with every teacher, then all relevant ratios are $2006/14$. This means $t \le 2006/14$. Now we will show that $t \ge 2006/14$.
For $1 \le i \le 14$, let $a_i$ denote the number of students who are acquainted with the $i$\text{th} teacher, and for $1 \le j \le 2006$, let $b_j$ denote the number of teachers who are acquainted with the $j$\text{th} student. Let $T$ be the set of ordered pairs $(i, j)$ of teachers and students who are acquainted with each other. Observe that with this notation we have $|\{j : (i, j) \in T\}| = a_i \ge 0$ and $|\{i : (i, j) \in T\}| = b_j \ge 1$.
Assume that $(i_o, j_o) \in T$ satisfies the condition $a_{i_o}/b_{j_o} \ge a_i/b_j$ for all $(i, j) \in T$. Adding the inequalities $a_{i_o}/b_{j_o} \cdot 1/a_i \ge 1/b_j$ for all $(i, j) \in T$ we obtain the inequality
$$
\frac{a_{i_o}}{b_{j_o}} \sum_{(i,j) \in T} \frac{1}{a_i} \ge \sum_{(i,j) \in T} \frac{1}{b_j}.
$$
Since
$$
\sum_{(i,j) \in T} \frac{1}{a_i} = \sum_{i=1}^{14} \sum_{\{j:(i,j) \in T\}} \frac{1}{a_i} = \sum_{\{i:a_i \ne 0\}} \frac{a_i}{a_i} = \sum_{\{i:a_i \ne 0\}} 1 \le 14,
$$
and similarly,
$$
\sum_{(i,j) \in T} \frac{1}{b_j} = \sum_{j=1}^{2006} \sum_{\{i:(i,j) \in T\}} \frac{1}{b_j} = \sum_{j=1}^{2006} \frac{b_j}{b_j} = \sum_{j=1}^{2006} 1 = 2006,
$$
we deduce that $a_{i_o}/b_{j_o} \ge 2006/14$, and hence $t \ge 2006/14$.

statement: Prove that there exists no triangle whose side lengths, area and angles (measured in degrees) are rational numbers.
solutions:
By the law of sines and the law of cosines, the sines and cosines of the angles of such a triangle are also rational. Therefore it suffices to prove that if $\theta$ is an angle whose degree measure is a rational number that is not an integer multiple of $90$, then both $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ cannot be rational.

Assume otherwise. Let $u, v$ and $w > 1$ be pairwise relatively prime integers such that $\sin\theta = u/w$, $\cos\theta = v/w$. $w$ cannot be even as $u^2 + v^2 \equiv w^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ (mod $4$) is not possible.

We will prove by induction that there exist integers $k_n$ such that $w^n \cos n\theta = 2^{n-1}v^n + k_n w^2$ for $n \ge 1$. $k_1 = 0$ works for $n = 1$. If $n = 2$, then $w^2 \cos 2\theta = w^2(2 \cos^2 \theta - 1) = 2v^2 - w^2$, and $k_2 = -1$ will do. For $n > 1$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
w^n \cos n\theta &= w^n(2 \cos \theta \cos (n-1)\theta - \cos (n-2)\theta) \\
&= 2v(2^{n-2}v^{n-1} + k_{n-1}w^2) - w^2(2^{n-3}v^{n-2} + k_{n-2}w^2) \\
&= 2^{n-1}v^n + (2vk_{n-1} - (2^{n-3}v^{n-2} + k_{n-2}w^2))w^2,
\end{aligned}
$$
and we can take $k_n = 2vk_{n-1} - (2^{n-3}v^{n-2} + k_{n-2}w^2)$.

Now choose a positive integer $n$ such that $\cos n\theta = 1$. Then $w^n = 2^{n-1}v^n + k_n w^2$. But, as $(w, 2v) = 1$ and $w > 1$, this is a contradiction.
